one_liner: Opt-in io_uring backend inside Asio/Boost.Asio that replaces the epoll reactor on Linux 5.10+ without API changes.
what_it_does: On Linux, Asio's io_context normally uses an epoll reactor to handle sockets, descriptors and timers. If you define ASIO_HAS_IO_URING and ASIO_DISABLE_EPOLL at compile time, Asio uses io_uring_service instead, so the same async_read_some/async_write_some/async_accept/timer code runs on io_uring without source changes. If you define only ASIO_HAS_IO_URING, sockets stay on epoll and io_uring handles only asio::stream_file and random_access_file, which need it on Linux.
how_it_is_fast: With epoll, each operation takes a readiness notification plus a separate read or write syscall. Here each async operation becomes a completion-based submission queue entry (SQE): IORING_OP_RECVMSG for receives, or READ_FIXED/WRITE_FIXED when buffers are registered. SQEs are batched: a posted submit operation flushes them, or they go out at once when 128 are pending (reactor/io_uring_submit_batch_size), so one io_uring_submit call covers many operations, and the run loop collects completions from the completion queue (CQ). An operation that returns would_block (for example, on an fd with O_NONBLOCK set) falls back to IORING_OP_POLL_ADD plus a non-blocking recv, which works like epoll.
when_to_use: Existing Asio or Boost.Asio code on Linux 5.10+ where you want io_uring from a recompile rather than a rewrite, and to A/B test it against epoll by flipping two macros.
A single-threaded io_context (concurrency_hint 1) driving many descriptors with small messages; the maintainer's test (300 pipes, 13-byte messages) finished about 1.38x faster in wall-clock time.
Async file I/O through asio::stream_file / random_access_file, which require io_uring on Linux anyway.
Workloads that can pre-register buffers (register_buffers), so reads and writes use io_uring's fixed-buffer READ_FIXED/WRITE_FIXED path.
when_not_to_use: When total CPU matters more than wall-clock time: the maintainer notes the benchmark leaves out io_uring kernel worker-thread CPU, and total CPU use was higher than with epoll.
On virtualised or WSL2 hosts without measuring first: one user's WSL2 run of the same benchmark had epoll faster (2.97 s vs 3.66 s).

A multi-threaded io_context on the default single ring: all threads share one SQ/CQ behind a mutex, and the maintainer said the backend works best single-threaded. Per-thread rings (reactor/io_uring_ring_count) only arrived in 1.38.2 (July 2026), and no published benchmark covers them.

Timer-heavy code with io_uring as the default backend: open issues report a steady_timer firing only once (#1530) and a timer segfault (#1349), and #1235 reports UBSan errors when an io_context used with coroutines is destroyed.
Non-Linux platforms or kernels older than 5.10: the build hits a compile-time #error below 5.10, and other OSes keep their usual backends.

integration.dependencies: liburing (headers at compile time, -luring at link time); Boost only if you use the Boost.Asio variant (BOOST_ASIO_HAS_IO_URING)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (Asio 1.29+); Linux kernel headers 5.10+; liburing (the io_uring_iowait option needs liburing 2.12+ and kernel 6.15+)
integration.platforms: Linux 5.10+ only; the backend has no architecture-specific code
integration.thread_safety: Same as Asio in general: an io_context may be run from several threads, and per-I/O-object locking is on by default (reactor/io_locking). By default all threads share one ring guarded by a mutex; from 1.38.2, reactor/io_uring_ring_count assigns each thread one of N rings, round-robin.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same Asio API and source, but the backend is chosen per build by macros (ASIO_HAS_IO_URING + ASIO_DISABLE_EPOLL), applies to the whole program, and the code has no runtime fallback to epoll

gotchas: Define ASIO_HAS_IO_URING the same way in every translation unit: it changes the recycling allocator's chunk_size (8 vs 4), and open issue #1635 reports a heap buffer overflow when units disagree. ASIO_ENABLE_VERSION_NAMESPACE puts the io_uring setting into the inline namespace name, so mismatched units do not share the same symbols.

Per the docs, ASIO_DISABLE_EPOLL on its own forces select. Only together with ASIO_HAS_IO_URING does it make io_uring the default (ASIO_HAS_IO_URING_AS_DEFAULT), and ASIO_HAS_IO_URING alone leaves sockets on epoll.

Each ring defaults to 16384 entries (reactor/io_uring_ring_size), which locks memory per ring; lower it where RLIMIT_MEMLOCK is small. If io_uring_queue_init fails, the service throws instead of falling back to epoll.

By default a thread waiting on the ring counts as iowait whenever SQEs are pending, including socket polls and timers, which inflates iowait metrics. Set reactor/io_uring_iowait=false (needs liburing 2.12+ and kernel 6.15+).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you already have Asio or Boost.Asio code and want io_uring without a rewrite. For new io_uring-first code, uring_exec reports 1.27x-3.46x the ping-pong throughput of Asio's io_uring backend, and Condy's recv benchmark only measured Asio's epoll path (1588 MB/s vs Condy's 2110 MB/s).
verified_claims_summary: In a 2021 comment on issue #401, the maintainer ran a single-threaded io_context over 100 rings of 3 pipes, passing a 13-byte message until each ring reached 10,000 iterations: 1.602 s wall-clock with epoll vs 1.158 s with the pre-release io_uring backend (about 1.38x), on Linux 5.10 with CPU, compiler and flags not stated. The io_uring figure leaves out kernel worker-thread CPU, and a 2022 WSL2 rerun (kernel 5.10.102.1, Boost 1.79) found epoll faster.
status_note: Actively maintained and BSL-1.0 licensed: the io_uring backend has shipped opt-in since Asio 1.21.0, 1.38.2 (July 2026) added multi-ring and batching settings, and one user reports four years of production use.
